Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: Margot Vance stood in the stainless-steel prep line of her restaurant, her hands steady only because they were busy. The assault had not happened in a dark alley, but in the quiet, dimly lit back office of a bistro where she had trusted a male supervisor she had known for years. When he had suddenly crossed a professional boundary and pinned her against the filing cabinet, the world collapsed into a single, suffocating pressure. Months later, she still could not put the frightening event into words. The memory refused to cohere; it lived only in disconnected pieces—a sharp scrape of a shoe, the sudden weight on her chest, the terrifying realization that her trust had been weaponized. That profound sense of betrayal seeped into her worldview, convincing her that kindness was merely a prelude to violation and that she could never again allow herself to be emotionally vulnerable with anyone. In the months that followed, Margot’s daily life narrowed as specific moments in her kitchen began to activate the past. When a supplier lingered to discuss business in her line of sight, or when a diner’s tone turned inquisitive, those unspoken sensory fragments would instantly surge forward. Her body would immediately lock into the exact posture of that night, shoulders hunched and breath shallow, as if the assault were physically occupying the space beside her. These triggered recollections quickly hardened into her core appraisals: people fundamentally could not be trusted, and safety was an illusion. The relentless return of these disjointed, wordless memories cemented her conviction that she had been deeply betrayed and that vulnerability was always a liability. As these appraisals took root, they completely recalibrated her perception of the ordinary world. Margot came to believe that strangers approaching her in the grocery store or walking up behind her in the kitchen aisle carried an unspoken threat. She found herself permanently on edge, scanning every corner and doorway, her nervous system braced for impact. This constant state of guarded alertness meant that even a sudden clatter of pans or a colleague’s quick step toward her station would make her jump as though attacked. Her core convictions about mistrust actively shaped how her mind returned to the assault, keeping the sensory pieces deliberately fragmented and refusing to let them cohere. These hardened beliefs actively manufactured new triggers, ensuring that any shift toward emotional closeness or certain conversation topics would immediately register as dangerous. Her hyperalertness kept the sensory pieces of the assault perpetually active, ensuring that any flash of unexpected movement would inevitably reinforce her conviction that harm was unpredictable and betrayal was inevitable. Each time she flinched at a stranger’s approach or bristled at a man’s proximity, the triggers sharpened, ensuring that certain topics and emotional intimacy would continue to pull her backward. Now, six years later, the loop had woven itself into the fabric of her profession and her marriage. Though her husband loved her, Margot kept him at an emotional distance, fearing that any deep connection would eventually unravel into the same violation. In the kitchen, she had begun avoiding the service floor entirely, unable to reconcile the sensory overload with the calm focus her staff expected. The concrete cost of her avoidance was visible in her declining leadership; she had lost her credibility during dinner service when she abruptly locked the walk-in freezer during a rush, refusing to let any male staff enter. What finally brought her to therapy was the exhaustion of constant vigilance and the dawning realization that her attempts to stay safe were systematically dismantling the life she had built. She was no longer hoping to forget the past; she simply wanted to stop living as if the office door were still closing behind her.
